Specifically, the receptive fields shown seem to all be responsive to a specific orientation and velocity. However, they are all "global" (or "large" scale), in the sense that they all have only one big contiguous area of positive weights along one big contiguous area of negative weights.

The question that naturally arises is whether the non-associative learning employed here can produce more refined patterns in the receptive fields, or whether it can learn to be sensitive over different scales of features by combining (at the level of the lobula) different large-scale receptive fields in non-trivial ways. Also, why do patterns learned, when scanning whole images, perform best when not applied to a whole image.

The reviewer acknowledges the difficulty in showing the receptive fields when they include both a spatial and temporal component, and as such also that this sensitivity on a varying scale could already be present in the network, as a combination of larger scale receptive fields (albeit the results with different speeds and different distances from the image seems to suggest some specificity in the scale of visual feature that the network can identify). This could warrant a more in-depth study of the performance of the proposed network architecture when varying the training set and training conditions (e.g., speed).

In-Line comments

L134-136: but is the scanning order selected by the model, or is it fixed? At the moment it seems to be implied that the 5 frames are given. Is there reason to assume this is the optimal order? Is there any optimal order? P.S. I see that this is touched upon below. See comment to L210-219

L185-188: Videos 1 and 2 are missing. I assume they are present in MaBouDi et al. 2021, but if they are referenced here with this indication they should be included. Alternatively, you could add in the text a general reference to the previous paper.

L196-197: writing here "during the initial experiment" seems to refer to the first experiment you are doing in this paper. Instead, it seems you want to refer to your previous paper. This should be made more clear.

Figure 2B – In the caption, there seem to be typos on what is rewarding and what is punishing.

200-201 – This wording may be interpreted as the model having active control, which is however not the case.

L201-219: statistical analysis should be done and reported. In an attempt to comparing this model with living animals, I believe every step should be taken to follow the same procedure. How many simulated bees have been tested in the + vs X task? Are they 20 per shape or 20 per scanning pattern? Is the data collected after how many visits? Reporting percentage is I believe insufficient, and a binomial test against chance level should be performed. This is the case for all experiments in this paper.

Figure 2B: is this SD or CI?

L210-219: the authors here refer to an initial poor performance. In figure 2C, is this the last two bars of the graph? This should be made clear.

Overall, the experiments here described aimed at finding the best scanning procedure, but I am not sure if how this was evaluated is appropriate. First, how is the training on natural images organized? Are they all scanned in the bottom half, left to right? If that is the case, the highest efficiency of lower-half scanning may be linked to the highest similarity to training, not to the real efficiency of the technique, and it would as such suggest low generalizability of the model. If instead training is repeated for all experiments following that presentation pattern, and thus the scanning procedure has an effect of learning effectiveness, this may be a property of this network, but not necessarily of living bees (as L216 somewhat suggests). It could in fact be a self-fulfilling prophecy (behavioral experiments suggest the need for scanning, the network is designed with a recurrent layer to enable shape reconstruction, and the network is most effective with scanning).

If you want to suggest that scanning from the bottom left is indeed more effective, you need to also include conditions other than the confirmatory one. These could be scanning right to left, or scanning left to right in the top half, or scanning top to bottom, or even diagonally (which I suspect are going to produce identical results). As of now, the experimental conditions only allow us to conclude that scanning sections is more effective than seeing the whole image, which again is to me included as a property of the network. Also, I may be wrong about this, but bees visual field is not centered frontally on the animal, but points upward (https://www.researchgate.net/publication/326717773_Bumblebee_visual_allometry_results_in_locally_improved_resolution_and_globally_improved_sensitivity). Being this the case, a bee moving across the bottom of a stimulus wouldn't it actually be looking at it fully, with the visual field centered on the horizontal symmetry line?

A similar reasoning should be made for scanning speed. Velocity is tangled with stimulus size. 0.1m/s may work best with this size but will change drastically depending on how much of the stimulus occupies the virtual bee visual field.

I want to point out that none of these points are detrimental to the effectiveness of the model itself, which seems to present good performances. But if claims want to be made about the best scanning strategy, especially if confronted with real animals, these points should be tested and addressed. As of now, we can say that the current model best performs under certain conditions, but we can't generalize the effectiveness of such conditions to be the best for the task, nor the best for bees.

L221-252: I believe also here binomial statistics should be produced. I understand it seems to be redundant for performances nearing 100%, but this becomes more relevant for the 60% and 40% reported in Fig3E. On the same note, specific values should be reported, both for averages and SD.

246-251 – Repetition of a period.

It would be helpful if Figure 3 also reported the real bees data, as taken from the various papers. This would give a sense of how closely the model follows the bees behavior. Of course, bees are more complex and are subject to, among others, motivational effects which will make the choice percentage less clean, but I still think this would be appreciable.

311-312 – "When the model is limited to only four neurons in the lobula, it lacks the capability to encode the entire spatio-temporal structure that is naturally present in the training patterns". This wording seems to suggest that with more neurons it can encode the entire spatio-temporal structure of the training patterns, which may be an overstatement.

L314-316: I agree that these neurons are sufficient for the discrimination task in hand, but I am unsure whether is appropriate to extend this to bees, as the paragraph title implies. Bees have to use the system to respond to much more complex patterns, like photorealistic ones. For example, is 16 neurons still enough for the face discrimination task?

355-356 – It is unclear how the study would suggest a crucial role of movement in the ability to efficiently analyze and encode the environment. In this work, movement of the input pattern is taken as a given condition under which the network is trained, and not as a tool that can be exploited to have an advantage in the encoding and analysis of the pattern itself.

Discussion: In general, I am not fully convinced that your model can say anything about the bees or the optimal performance in general, but should focus on the effectiveness of the model itself. This is because of what I have reported above about how the model performance is at least partially dependent on the model design, and not on how bees actually behave (which is hypothesized)

374-375 – In these lines, it is claimed that the model acts as a linear generative model, however, this is not shown in the results and these generative capabilities are not demonstrated.

487 – Calling $r_l^{La}$ as "the output of one lamina neuron" instead of "one lamina neuron" could improve clarity.

498 – I have not clear what "however" refers to, in this context

498 – Similarly. Rewording "the input of the m −the medulla neuron is calculated" to something like "the input to the $m$-th medulla neuron, $I_m{Me}$, is calculated as"

506-507 – Could reference to Figure 3B be a typo?

528-530 "At each step of training, a set of five patches with size 75x75 pixels, selected by shifting 15 pixels over the image from the left or right or the reverse orientation (Figures1B, 2A), was considered as the input of the model." This wording could be a bit confusing, especially as, coincidentally, 15*5=75. It could be improved to make it clear that one input to the network is (a concatenation?) of 5 patches of 75x75 pixels each, obtained by shifting a window of 75x75 pixels by 15 pixels, 5 times (if this is actually the case).

results.result: The model architecture implements a biologically-inspired visual processing pathway with sequential patch sampling (5 patches of 75×75 pixels at 0.1 m/s), feedforward connectivity from photoreceptors through lamina and medulla to lobula neurons, temporal integration with structured delays, and lateral inhibitory connections between lobula neurons. The connectivity is hypothesized to be refined through non-associative learning on time-varying natural images.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C29 provide detailed architectural specifications that are internally consistent and supported by references to figures. C30 explicitly frames the learning mechanism as a hypothesis, which is appropriate for a computational model. The model design is clearly described with specific parameters.

results.result: After training on natural images, lobula neurons in the model develop spatiotemporal orientation selectivity with elongated on/off receptive fields, demonstrate specificity to orientation (e.g., 150° tuned neuron firing at 26 spikes/sec), direction, contrast, and velocity, with responses closely resembling biological observations in bees and insects. Only a small subset of neurons respond to any given stimulus, indicating sparse and decorrelated activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C40 and C92 describe quantitative model results with specific firing rates, orientations, and tuning properties, supported by multiple figure references (2A-E). The comparison to biological data (C34, C39, C40) is appropriately cited. The sparse coding observation (C35) is consistent with the reported results.

results.result: Increasing the number of lobula neurons in the model enhances the diversity of orientation-selective responses and enables finer encoding of orientations and motion patterns through more distributed tuning properties.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C42 describe scalability results supported by supplementary figures. The relationship between neuron number and encoding precision is a logical consequence of the model architecture and is presented with appropriate figure references.

results.result: Training on natural images produces highly decorrelated lobula neuron responses (strong diagonal correlation matrix) and significantly reduces the sparseness index, indicating selective and efficient coding. Training on shuffled natural images produces only moderate sparseness reduction and non-structured receptive fields, demonstrating that spatial structure in training images is essential for efficient feature encoding.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C47 describe quantitative results from training experiments with appropriate controls (shuffled images). Figure 3 supports the correlation and sparseness measurements. The interpretation that spatial structure is necessary (C46-C47) is justified by the control experiment showing different outcomes with shuffled vs. natural images.

results.result: After associative learning training, the MBON exhibits reduced activity to rewarded patterns (plus sign) and increased activity to punished patterns (multiplication sign), successfully discriminating between them. A control model with fixed random connectivity in the visual lobe fails to discriminate, and the MBON response pattern is consistent with biological PE1 neurons in honeybee mushroom bodies.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C52 describe the associative learning results with appropriate controls (C51) and biological validation (C52). Figure 4B supports the MBON response dynamics. The comparison to biological data (Okada et al., 2007) strengthens the result.

results.result: Model performance in discriminating plus from multiplication patterns depends critically on scanning parameters: scanning only the lower half or lower left corner achieves ≥96-98% accuracy, while whole-pattern scanning achieves only 63%, increased speed reduces accuracy to 70%, stationary scanning achieves 60%, and training from >100mm distance results in failure. This aligns with real bee behavior of approaching stimuli closely with initially random choices.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C56 describe systematic parameter variations with quantitative performance metrics supported by Figure 4C and citations to bee behavior studies. The results demonstrate the importance of active vision and are consistent with biological observations (C56).

results.result: Scanning the lower half of patterns at normal speed produces stronger, more selective lobula neuron activation in a smaller subset compared to whole-pattern scanning, which produces more widespread overlapping activation. Neural responses show significantly larger angular distance (better separability) when scanning is restricted to the lower half versus whole pattern.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C60 describe comparative analysis of scanning strategies with quantitative measures (angular distance) supported by Figure 5. The results logically follow from the model architecture and demonstrate how scanning behavior affects neural representation quality.

results.result: The model successfully discriminates various pattern types including angled bars, rotated crosses, spirals, gratings, oriented bars in quadrants (>99% accuracy on training, 61% on simplified variants), and human faces. It demonstrates generalization to novel patterns and implements both reward learning and rejection behavior (22% lower preference for negatively trained vs. novel patterns). Both real and simulated bees fail on 180° rotated faces.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C66 describe performance across multiple tasks with specific accuracy values and appropriate comparisons to biological data. Figure 6 supports these results. The generalization capability (C62) and rejection behavior (C63) demonstrate sophisticated learning beyond simple discrimination.

results.result: The model fails to replicate bee performance on complex patterns from Stach et al. 2004 that require recognizing spatial arrangements of orientations across four quadrants, despite successfully discriminating plus from multiplication signs when scanning whole patterns.
results.evaluation: Claim C67 honestly reports a model limitation supported by Figure 6F. The authors acknowledge this failure and discuss it as indicating the model lacks mechanisms for integrating local features into global representations, which is appropriate scientific reporting.

results.result: Reducing the number of lobula neurons decreases variability in spatiotemporal receptive fields and overall model performance. With only 4 neurons, the model cannot encode full spatiotemporal structure (only vertical/horizontal fields). With 16 neurons, the model discriminates moderately complex patterns but fails on highly complex stimuli like human faces.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C71 describe systematic ablation studies varying neuron number, supported by Figure 7 and videos. The results logically demonstrate the relationship between network capacity and task complexity, with appropriate quantitative performance data.

results.result: Fixed (non-plastic) inhibitory connections between lobula neurons limit the ability to encode moving orientations, indicating that plasticity of inhibitory interneurons plays a crucial role in efficient visual representation.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C73 describe a control experiment (fixed vs. plastic inhibition) supported by Figure 8 and Video 6. The interpretation (C73) is justified by the experimental manipulation showing reduced encoding capacity without inhibitory plasticity.

results.result: The model demonstrates that active scanning and non-associative learning dynamically shape neural activity to optimize information flow. Lobula neurons self-organize into orientation-selective cells with sparse, decorrelated responses encoding orientations biased by speed and contrast, suggesting co-evolution with scanning behavior. The model's robust pattern recognition performance implies similar encoding mechanisms may exist in insects.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C77 summarize the main findings of the study, integrating results from multiple experiments. C76 appropriately frames co-evolution as a suggestion rather than proven fact. C77's implication about biological systems is reasonable given the model's performance and biological validation throughout, though it remains an inference.

results.result: Bumblebees have compound eyes with ~5500 ommatidia containing three photoreceptor types (UV, blue, green wavelength sensitive), with green photoreceptors predominantly mediating visual pattern recognition, justifying the model's focus on green channel input.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C80 state biological facts supported by appropriate citations and provide justification for modeling decisions. These are well-established facts in the literature used to ground the model design.

results.result: The model was trained using 50,000 time-varying image patches randomly sampled from 100 natural flower and scene images during lateral scanning, with synaptic weights in the optic lobe updated through this exposure.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C83 describe the training procedure with specific quantitative details. This is a straightforward methodological description supported by references to Methods and figures.

results.result: The model implements associative learning in mushroom bodies using dopamine-modulated STDP for negative patterns and a novel octopamine-modulated STDP rule (hypothesized to induce synaptic depression) for positive patterns. This is grounded in biological evidence that mushroom bodies are critical for insect learning, that KC-MBON synapses follow Hebbian STDP (though STDP alone is insufficient), that octopamine and dopamine signal appetitive/aversive values, and that octopamine depresses STDP synapses. The resulting MBON responses match PE1 neurons in honeybee brains.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C91 describe the associative learning implementation with extensive biological grounding through citations (C86-C90). C85 appropriately presents the octopamine rule as a hypothesis. C91 validates the model output against biological data. The biological foundation is strong, though C85's novel mechanism requires experimental validation.

results.result: Bees demonstrate remarkable visual learning capabilities including associating colors/orientations with rewards, categorizing patterns by identifying relevant features, grasping abstract concepts, and solving numerosity tasks through sequential scanning. However, it remains unclear how bees achieve complex pattern recognition despite low visual acuity and limited neural resources.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C6 provide background on bee cognitive abilities supported by extensive citations. C6 appropriately identifies a knowledge gap that motivates the study. These are well-established facts in the bee cognition literature.

results.result: Natural scenes have different statistical structure than artificial ones, and visual neurons are hypothesized to exploit these regularities for efficient encoding. Insect visual neurons have evolved mechanisms providing robust responses to naturalistic inputs, with fly photoreceptors extracting more information from natural time series than artificial stimuli. Insect sensory pathways dynamically adapt to environmental conditions, with experience-dependent adaptation observed in photoreceptors and motion-sensitive neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C14 provide theoretical and empirical background on efficient coding and neural adaptation, all supported by appropriate citations. C8 correctly identifies Barlow's hypothesis as a hypothesis. The claims establish the theoretical framework for the study.

results.result: Active sampling strategies are widely observed across species, with primates using eye movements and insects using head/body movements to optimize visual processing. Bees engage in systematic scanning movements to construct neural representations, enumerate elements sequentially rather than in parallel, and prioritize specific pattern regions before decisions, overcoming limitations in discriminating similar hues in brief flashes.
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C22 establish the importance of active vision across species and specifically in bees, all supported by extensive citations. These provide the behavioral foundation motivating the model's focus on scanning behavior.
